These are not graded, but you should attempt them all before the quiz. Try each question yourself first, then expand the **Solution** to check.

## Additional Examples

**1.** Utility maximization. Consider the problem
$$\max_{\{x_1, x_2\}} \quad x_1^{\alpha} x_2^{\beta} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = m$$
where $p_1$ and $p_2$ are the prices of goods 1 and 2, and $m$ is the income available to spend on the two goods. Find the optimal $x_1^*$ and $x_2^*$.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The Lagrange function is
$$\mathcal{L}(x_1, x_2, \lambda) = x_1^{\alpha} x_2^{\beta} + \lambda(m - p_1 x_1 - p_2 x_2)$$
with first-order conditions
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_1} &= \alpha x_1^{\alpha - 1} x_2^{\beta} - \lambda p_1 = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_2} &= \beta x_1^{\alpha} x_2^{\beta - 1} - \lambda p_2 = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} &= m - p_1 x_1 - p_2 x_2 = 0
\end{aligned}$$
Dividing the first condition by the second,
$$\frac{\alpha x_1^{\alpha - 1} x_2^{\beta}}{\beta x_1^{\alpha} x_2^{\beta - 1}} = \frac{p_1}{p_2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\alpha x_2}{\beta x_1} = \frac{p_1}{p_2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x_2 = \frac{\beta}{\alpha} \cdot \frac{p_1}{p_2} \cdot x_1$$
Substituting into the constraint,
$$m - p_1 x_1 - \frac{\beta}{\alpha} p_1 x_1 = m - p_1 x_1 \left(1 + \frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x_1^* = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta} \cdot \frac{m}{p_1}$$
and then
$$x_2^* = \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} \cdot \frac{m}{p_2}$$

</details>

**2.** Cost minimization. A firm chooses capital $K$ and labor $L$ to produce a fixed quantity $\bar{Q}$ at the lowest cost, where $p$ is the price of capital and $w$ is the price of labor:
$$\min_{\{K, L\}} \quad pK + wL \quad \text{s.t.} \quad Q(K, L) = \bar{Q}$$
Set up the Lagrange function, write down the first-order conditions, and find the two conditions that the optimal $K^*$ and $L^*$ satisfy.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The Lagrange function is
$$\mathcal{L}(K, L, \lambda) = pK + wL + \lambda\left(\bar{Q} - Q(K, L)\right)$$
with first-order conditions
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K} &= p - \lambda Q_K(K, L) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial L} &= w - \lambda Q_L(K, L) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} &= \bar{Q} - Q(K, L) = 0
\end{aligned}$$
where $Q_K = \partial Q / \partial K$ and $Q_L = \partial Q / \partial L$. Dividing the first condition by the second, the optimal $K^*$ and $L^*$ satisfy
$$\frac{Q_K(K^*, L^*)}{Q_L(K^*, L^*)} = \frac{p}{w} \qquad \text{and} \qquad Q(K^*, L^*) = \bar{Q}$$

</details>

**3.** Intertemporal utility maximization. Your utility from consumption $c_1$ in period 1 and $c_2$ in period 2 is
$$U(c_1, c_2) = \ln c_1 + \beta \ln c_2 \qquad 0 < \beta < 1$$
You earn income $y_1 > 0$ in period 1 and $y_2 > 0$ in period 2, and any income $s$ you save in period 1 earns interest $r > 0$, so $c_1 + s = y_1$ and $c_2 = y_2 + (1 + r)s$. Combining these, your budget constraint is
$$c_1 + \frac{1}{1+r} c_2 = m, \qquad \text{where } m = y_1 + \frac{1}{1+r} y_2$$
is your present-discounted income.

a. Write down the Lagrange function and the first-order conditions.

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$$L(c_1, c_2, \lambda) = \ln c_1 + \beta \ln c_2 + \lambda\left(m - c_1 - \frac{1}{1+r} c_2\right)$$
First-order conditions:
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c_1} &= \frac{1}{c_1} - \lambda = 0 \\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c_2} &= \frac{\beta}{c_2} - \frac{\lambda}{1+r} = 0 \\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \lambda} &= m - c_1 - \frac{1}{1+r} c_2 = 0
\end{aligned}$$

</details>

b. Find the optimal $c_1^*$, $c_2^*$, and $\lambda^*$.

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The first condition gives $\lambda^* = 1/c_1^*$. Substituting into the second, $\beta / c_2^* = 1 / \left((1+r) c_1^*\right)$, so
$$c_2^* = \beta(1+r) c_1^*$$
Substituting into the constraint,
$$c_1^* + \frac{1}{1+r} \beta(1+r) c_1^* = m \quad \Rightarrow \quad c_1^* = \frac{m}{1 + \beta}$$
Then
$$c_2^* = \frac{\beta(1+r) m}{1 + \beta} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lambda^* = \frac{1}{c_1^*} = \frac{1 + \beta}{m}$$

</details>

c. How does the maximum utility $U^*$ change when present-discounted income $m$ increases slightly?

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The Lagrange multiplier measures how the optimal value changes when the constraint is relaxed:
$$\frac{dU^*}{dm} = \lambda^* = \frac{1 + \beta}{m} > 0$$
So utility rises with income, by $(1 + \beta)/m$ per extra unit, and by less the richer you already are.

</details>
